page_intro: The lab works on one disease in depth, and on the two kinds of evidence that let us study it properly. Each area below began with a question we could not answer using what already existed, either because the data had never been assembled, the measurement had never been validated, or the mechanics had never been tested.
a1_p1: The gluteus medius and minimus sit on the side of the hip and hold the pelvis level when you stand on one leg. When their tendons degenerate or tear, the result is pain on the outside of the hip, a limp, and difficulty sleeping on that side. It affects roughly one in six adults over 50, most often women in their fifties and sixties, and it is routinely written off as bursitis and treated with a steroid injection. The tendon is usually the real problem. Different groups have described the same tear under competing names and rarely cite one another, so the literature that ought to settle how to diagnose and treat it does not add up to a coherent picture. No outcome instrument has been validated for these patients, and no payment model has been built around the condition.
a1_p2: Our work is an attempt to build that missing evidence base from the ground up. We started by collecting every published description of the lesion, nine studies using competing acronyms, and reconciling them into a single account of what is actually being described. We are asking who develops it, using a cohort of 385,868 women to test whether hormone therapy after menopause changes the risk and whether the timing of starting it matters. We assessed every outcome instrument used in this population against formal measurement standards, since most were designed for hip replacement rather than tendon repair, and we are testing which MRI findings predict which parts of recovery rather than recovery in general. We pooled the treatment literature, from physical therapy through injections to open and endoscopic repair, into one staged pathway. The end of it is a consensus process with radiologists, primary care physicians, and physical therapists to settle the naming and the diagnostic criteria for the field rather than for one group.
a2_p1: Most questions in orthopaedics never get a randomized trial. The conditions are too uncommon, the outcomes take a decade to appear, and a trial large enough to answer the question would cost more than anyone will pay, so surgeons fall back on experience and on studies of a few hundred patients from a single hospital. There is a second limitation of trials that gets less attention. A trial reports an average. If a treatment helps one group of patients a great deal and does nothing for everyone else, the average comes out small, the treatment is judged ineffective, and the group it helped is never identified.
a2_p2: Health records now cover tens of millions of patients, which is enough to reach questions a trial cannot. The difficulty is that this data was produced by care rather than by research, so it is full of traps: patients who look healthier because they were selected for treatment, follow-up that simply stops when someone changes insurer, and associations that reflect referral patterns rather than biology. A good part of this work is methodological, controlling those problems well enough that the answer means something. We use these networks to screen dozens of medications at once for association with arthritis, to compare how implants survive in patients with cerebral palsy or multiple sclerosis against patients with ordinary arthritis, and to link databases that have not previously been combined. We also measure what care costs from the bottom up, timing each step of an operation rather than accepting the hospital's accounting, because what a procedure is charged and what it consumes are different numbers.
a2_p3: The same records make a different kind of question possible. Orthopaedic journals now publish machine learning models constantly, predicting complications, reading radiographs, estimating who will benefit from an operation, and very few are ever tested on data from a hospital other than the one that produced them. Models usually perform substantially worse when they are. We are running published algorithms against data they have never seen, both to find out which survive and to work out what separates those that do from those that do not. The tooling matters as much as the analysis: assembling a cohort from messy clinical records used to take months of manual chart review, and we build and evaluate software agents to do that work in a form we can audit.
a3_p1: A surgeon repairing a torn tendon decides how many anchors to use, where to place them, and whether to reinforce the repair with a graft or a synthetic patch. Those decisions are mechanical, and they are mostly made by feel, because there is no way to try them on a patient. Repairs of the hip abductors fail often enough to matter, and the use of scaffolds to reinforce them has grown quickly without much evidence about which patients they actually help.
a3_p2: We build computer models of individual patients from scans they have already had, so the geometry, the tear, and the state of the muscle belong to that person rather than to an average. The model shows where load concentrates and which part of a construct is carrying it, which is usually where a repair begins to fail. Because a simulation is only as good as its assumptions, we test the same constructs in cadaveric tissue, which is harder than it sounds: the muscle tears out of the clamp before the repair itself fails, so measuring the strength of a repair means first solving the problem of holding onto the muscle. The longer aim is a model that runs quickly enough to inform a decision during a clinic visit instead of over several days.
a3_fig_caption: How much load a tendon repair holds before it fails, with and without a scaffold.
a3_p3: The third way to study mechanics is to measure them during the operation itself. A robotic knee replacement produces a plan before the first cut, then records what was actually measured once the surgeon is inside the joint, and almost none of that record is examined afterwards. Around one in five patients remains dissatisfied after a knee replacement, a figure that has barely moved in twenty years, and the usual explanation is a knee that was not balanced well. We treat the robot's plan as a prediction and check it against what the surgeon found. It underestimates the gap on the inner side of the knee, and the error grows the more bowed the leg was to begin with, which is correctable in the moment once you know it is there.

open_problems.title: Predicting which abductor tendon repairs fail
open_problems.desc: Gluteus medius repairs fail at meaningful rates, and outcomes vary widely. Using imaging, intraoperative findings, and longitudinal outcomes from our repair cohort, the goal is a model that identifies repairs at high risk of failure and the factors that drive it.
open_problems.needs: Data: imaging, operative, outcomes · Methods: ML, survival analysis

open_problems.title: From intraoperative data to a structured operative record
open_problems.desc: Robotic platforms log detailed data for every case, but little of it reaches surgical registries because the translation is manual. The problem is an agentic pipeline that converts intraoperative and EHR data into structured, auditable documentation a surgeon would sign.
open_problems.needs: Data: robotic logs, EHR · Methods: LLM agents, FHIR

open_problems.title: Separating cause from association in drug-osteoarthritis screens
open_problems.desc: A medication-wide screen surfaces many drugs associated with osteoarthritis. Association is not cause. The work is to take the strongest signals and test them with negative controls, target-trial emulation, and sensitivity analysis to see what holds.
open_problems.needs: Data: federated EHR · Methods: causal inference, pharmacoepidemiology

open_problems.title: A fast surrogate for patient-specific finite element analysis
open_problems.desc: A full finite element model of a repair construct takes hours to build and solve. A learned surrogate that predicts the stress field from imaging in seconds, accurately enough to inform a decision, would make this usable in clinic.
open_problems.needs: Data: imaging, FE models · Methods: surrogate modeling, geometry processing

open_problems.title: Correcting the robot's gap prediction across deformity
open_problems.desc: Robotic knee replacement underpredicts the medial gap as native coronal deformity increases. The problem is to characterize that error across the full deformity range and build a correction a surgeon can use intraoperatively.
open_problems.needs: Data: robotic arthroplasty · Methods: modeling, data science

open_problems.title: A reproducible classification for concealed abductor tears
open_problems.desc: Undersurface abductor tears sit beneath intact superficial fibers and are described in the literature under competing names. The work is an imaging-based, reproducible classification, ideally with automated segmentation, that the field can use consistently.
open_problems.needs: Data: MRI · Methods: segmentation, clinical research
